vignette:
Kofi always believed his mind was his sharpest tool, a finely calibrated instrument that saw patterns others missed. At nineteen, he was the youngest detective at the firm, a prodigy whose ambition was matched only by his results. He moved through the humid, bustling streets of Accra with a confidence that bordered on arrogance. He was tracking a smuggling ring—a case that felt like a final exam, the one that would prove he was more than just a kid with a knack for puzzles. It was this confidence that got him caught. One miscalculation, one overlooked detail, and the world shrank to the suffocating dark of a shipping container at the port.

He was inside for four days. Time dissolved into a cycle of thirst, the clang of the metal door, and the disembodied voices that interrogated him. He learned to map the container by touch: the corrugated ridges of the walls, the splintered floorboards, the two small air holes near the ceiling that offered no light, only the scent of salt and diesel. He stopped being Kofi, the brilliant detective. He became a thing, a piece of cargo, his mind turning from a tool of investigation to a cage for his terror. When the police finally broke the lock, the sudden flood of daylight was so violent it felt like an attack.

That was six months ago. Now, the world outside feels like the lie. The real world is corrugated metal and darkness. He’s back at his small apartment, the one he shares with his girlfriend, Amara, but he’s not really there. He sits for hours at his desk, staring at cold case files, the words swimming into meaningless shapes. His boss is patient, telling him to take his time, but Kofi sees the pity in his eyes. He feels like a fraud. The boy detective, broken by the first real test.

Sleep offers no escape. He’s afraid to close his eyes, because that’s when the container rebuilds itself around him. He wakes up thrashing, the smell of rust thick in his nostrils, his own scream caught in his throat. Amara will try to hold him, but his body goes rigid. Her touch feels like a trap, her presence another set of walls closing in. He sees the hurt in her face when he pulls away, and a wave of shame washes over him, so cold and vast it feels like drowning.

During the day, he is a ghost in his own life. A truck rumbling down the street sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his heart hammering against his ribs as he scans for an escape route. The click of their apartment door locking at night sounds like the final, echoing clang of the container door. He can no longer go to the market; the press of the crowd, the shouting vendors, the feeling of being surrounded, sends him retreating back to the perceived safety of his rooms.

He spends most of his time tracing the patterns on the wall, his mind replaying every second of his captivity. He dissects his mistakes, the moments of hubris that led him there. *If only I had waited for backup. If only I hadn’t trusted the informant.* The thoughts are a relentless, punishing loop. He was supposed to be the one who saw everything, but he had been blind.

Last night, Amara tried to talk to him again, her voice soft and pleading. “Kofi, please. Let me in.” He looked at her, at this woman he loved, and felt nothing but a vast, empty distance. He couldn't find the words to explain that he was still locked in that dark, metal box, and he was terrified that if she got too close, he would somehow pull her in with him. So he just shook his head, turned away, and stared out the window, watching the city lights blur into a meaningless smear.
